newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: NZ CONCERNED ABOUT DOLE WAIT IN AUSTRALIA
The Prime Minister says he's sure concerns across the Tasman about New Zealanders having to wait two years for welfare in Australia can be worked through intelligently.
New migrants now have to wait two years instead of six months to receive welfare payments in Australia.
New Zealand's Prime Minister, Jim Bolger, says the move represents a significant policy shift and his government will be looking at the ramifications of the change.
John Howard says the policy has to be applied in a non-discriminatory fashion and New Zealanders can't be exempt.
But he says but the Government will honour the processes laid down in reciprocal social security agreements between the two countries.
ARNOTTS' WORKERS APPEAL TO EXTORTIONIST
The union covering Arnotts workers says the person behind the extortion attempt is ruining the livelihoods of the biscuit company employees.

Don Brown of the Miscellaneous Workers' Union was speaking as about 250 casual workers in Brisbane and Adelaide were stood down today, because production is affected by the threat to poison Arnotts' products.
Mr Brown says 250 permanent staff in Brisbane have been told to take leave.
He's appealed to those responsible for the extortion threat to reconsider their actions.
Export and interstate orders have assured continued production by Arnotts in New South Wales.
Minister seeks reward for tracking extortionist
Queensland's Police Minister Russell Cooper will ask the State Cabinet tomorrow to approve a 50-thousand dollar reward for information that helps catch the extortionist targetting Arnotts Biscuits.
Mr Cooper says the police investigation has reached a point where police believe the time is right to offer a reward.
He says a factor in the offer is that the deadline has arrived today at which the extortionist said biscuits would be poisoned if demands were not met.
The Minister says at this stage he doesn't expect the New South Wales Government to match Queensland's reward offer.
PRIVATE HEALTH INSURANCE DECLINE "STEADYING"
The Federal Government says the decline in private health insurance membership is steadying.
The Health Minister, Michael Wooldridge, says the December quarter figures show membership declined by only point three of one percent.
He says the drop is significantly less than the long term trend.
The Minister is taking the figures as a sign people are anticipating the Government's private health insurance incentives which come into effect in July.
He says the figures show the Government's incentive strategy is on the right track.
TWO DENY DEMANDING MONEY FROM COMEDIAN
Two men have pleaded not guilty in the Territory Supreme Court in Darwin today to allegations they demanded money from Perth comedian Kevin Bloody Wilson nearly three years ago.
50-year-old John Morris Kelly and 45-year-old Bryan James Clark are both charged with demanding with menaces ten thousand dollars after an incident on November the 17th in 1994.
Crown Prosecutor Michael Carey said Mr Kelly took offence to a song performed by the comedian at the Darwin Casino and said if he didn't pay he would put a curse on his family.
The trial is set down for four days before Justice Stephen Bailey.
BURKE'S TRIAL TO CONTINUE
The stealing trial of former West Australian Premier, Brian Burke, is to continue following the rejection of a submission by the defence that there was no case to answer.
District Court Judge George Sadleir ruled the prosecution had produced sufficient evidence to support the allegations against Mr Burke.
The former Premier is accused of stealing between 70 thousand and one hundred and 22 thousand dollars in campaign donations from the Labor Party while he was Premier between 1984 and 1988.
Mr Burke has denied the allegations and will give evidence in his own defence later today.
AUSTRALIANS ARE PRIME MOVERS
Australians are among the most mobile people in the world .. according to a report published in the Journal of Australian Population Association.

It says, on average, Australians move house more than 11 times during their lives -- which is similar to mobility in New Zealand, Canada and the United States, but almost double that in Britain, Ireland and Europe.
Author, Dr Martin Bell says it's a product of more fluid housing and job markets and may also be a hangover from the high mobility habits of our immigrant forbears.
He says unemployed people make twice as many moves as working people .. countering the common view that they're unwilling to move to find work.
